title: The beam in your eye
hook: first cast out the beam out of thine own eye (Matthew 7:3–5)
tomorrow: what does a house on rock sound like in a storm?

segments.voice: Yesterday: where my heart is, following the treasure, and a rich young man who went away sorrowful. Today the sermon hands you a mirror.

Scroll any comment section long enough and someone types "judge not" in the middle of judging somebody. Matthew 7 opens with it: "Judge not, that ye be not judged." So, yesterday's question: can you judge anyone at all? Christians read it two ways, and both have a case. But first, a king who judged a stranger's crime in a heartbeat, and missed his own.
screen: `JUDGE NOT, MID-JUDGMENT.` → `TWO READINGS.` → `A KING WHO MISSED HIS OWN.`

segments.voice: In Second Samuel, King David has taken another man's wife and covered it up with that man's death. The prophet Nathan comes with a story. A rich man with huge flocks has a guest to feed, so he takes a poor man's one little ewe lamb, a lamb the poor man raised like a daughter. David is furious: "the man that hath done this thing shall surely die." And Nathan says, "Thou art the man." David saw the speck in a stranger and missed the beam in himself. Jesus's picture: "why beholdest thou the mote that is in thy brother's eye, but considerest not the beam that is in thine own eye?" A speck of sawdust in your brother's eye, a roof timber in yours. Now the two readings. One says judge not means just that: leave condemning to God, because "with what measure ye mete, it shall be measured to you again." Its best case: Jesus opens with the plain command, and the beam story shows how blind a judge can be. The other reading points to the end of the passage: "first cast out the beam out of thine own eye; and then shalt thou see clearly to cast out the mote out of thy brother's eye." Its best case: Jesus expects you to help with the mote, and later in the chapter says "by their fruits ye shall know them." Both agree on the order. The beam comes first.
screen: `NATHAN: THOU ART THE MAN.` · `A SPECK, A ROOF TIMBER.` · `LEAVE JUDGING TO GOD.` · `BEAM FIRST, THEN HELP.` · then, large: `MY OWN BEAM.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes and bring to mind one person whose fault you see clearly. Then, gently, turn it around: is there a smaller or bigger version of the same thing in you? Sit with what you find, without a verdict either way.
The beam in your eye: the fault you miss in yourself while you're squinting at the speck in someone else's.
screen: `THE BEAM IN YOUR EYE — today's word`.

segments.voice: For the road: my own beam, before anyone else's mote. Nathan's four words still work.

screen: `DAY 1452 COUNTS.` → `NEW LINE: MY OWN BEAM · THE SERMON ON THE MOUNT, 6 OF 7.` → `TOMORROW: WHAT DOES A HOUSE ON ROCK SOUND LIKE IN A STORM?`

howItsDone: Christians differ on how to read 'judge not' (Matthew 7:1–5): some stress leaving judgment to God, others stress self-examination first and then honest, gentle correction. In Catholic practice, an examination of conscience comes before confession.
